clue.text: Old male cat occupying bronze padded seat

parts.note: O is the standard crossword shorthand for old

indicators.note: An army occupying a country is sitting inside its borders, so the cat's letters are placed within the ones that follow.

parts.note: bronze is a brownish colour as well as a metal, and a tan is that shade of skin
a tom is a male cat, and it slots in after the opening letter of that colour

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a stray asleep on the furniture. Bronze wants to be a metal and it is a colour, which is the one swap the clue turns on; the seat itself is the Turkish footstool that took the empire's name.
explanation.definitionFit: An ottoman is a low upholstered seat or footstool without a back, padded over the whole of its top.

clue.text: Definite nasty bug in donut

indicators.note: A nasty piece of work cannot be relied on to behave, and letters in that state will not stay in the order they were handed over in.

parts.note: three letters for the pile, taken for their spelling and not the insect
'in' is fodder as well, not the joinery it looks like, so seven more letters go in

explanation.walkthrough: The little word 'in' reads as a place — a bug inside a doughnut — and it is really two more letters for the shuffle. Leave it out and the count comes up short of ten.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone undoubting holds no doubt whatever, which is what being definite about a thing amounts to.

clue.text: Nick cheers on vacuous karaoke

indicators.note: In a down clue one thing resting on another is above it, so the thanks are stacked over what comes next.

parts.note: 'ta' is the everyday British thank-you, and 'cheers' is used for exactly the same purpose

indicators.note: A vacuous remark has nothing whatever inside it, so the word keeps only its first and last letters.

parts.note: only the outer pair survives, the opening letter and the closing one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' is the British slang verb for stealing rather than a name, and until you see that the clue looks like a man being cheered at a karaoke bar.
explanation.definitionFit: To nick something is British slang for stealing it, and to take is the plain verb sitting underneath the slang.

clue.text: Dismiss son, nothing to add over fine

indicators.note: In a down entry whatever is over something else sits above it, so the first pieces stack on top of the last one.

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son on a family tree
'end of' is the British way of saying there is no more to be said on the subject
F is the pencil grade meaning fine, and the usual shorthand for the word

explanation.walkthrough: British speech closes an argument with 'end of', meaning nothing more can be added, and the setter buries that phrase in a sentence about a family. The comma after 'son' is punctuation for the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: To send someone off is to dismiss them — the referee's word for ordering a player from the pitch, and the general sense of packing anyone away.

clue.text: As things transpired, where athletes would compete

definitions.meaning: the storyteller's phrase for how something actually turned out, as against what was expected
read literally: an event is one item on an athletics programme, the 100 metres or the high jump

explanation.walkthrough: The same three words are handed over twice with only a comma between them, once as an idiom about outcomes and once as a plain statement of place. No letters move at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means 'as it turned out', while the literal reading puts you inside a contest on the programme — one phrase, two senses.

clue.text: Spanish American silver peso found in corduroys

indicators.note: Something found in a place was already sitting there untouched, so the letters are lifted out of the word exactly as they stand.

parts.note: four consecutive letters sit inside this single word, beginning after its third

explanation.walkthrough: One word hides the whole thing, which is why no join is visible anywhere. A duro was the old five-peseta piece, the Spanish dollar that circulated across the colonies.
explanation.definitionFit: A duro is the Spanish silver dollar of eight reals, the coin that served as the peso through Spain's American territories.

clue.text: Shell of areca (betel) nuts fit for consumption

indicators.note: Someone who goes nuts loses all order and control, and letters in that condition have to be put back in some other arrangement.
A shell is what remains once the inside has gone, so only the first and last letters of the word survive.

parts.note: its outer pair, the opening letter and the closing one, with everything between discarded
five more letters, taken whole for their spelling rather than the palm they name

explanation.walkthrough: Areca and betel are the same nut chewed across South Asia, so the surface names one thing twice — and both words are there to be taken apart, not understood.
explanation.definitionFit: Something eatable is fit to be eaten, the plainer twin of edible, said of food that will do you no harm.

clue.text: Wild goat seen in prehistoric period

indicators.note: A wild animal answers to nobody, and letters described that way refuse to keep the order they arrived in.

parts.note: four letters taken for their spelling; the animal itself never appears
the other four, joined to the first set before anything is rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild goat' reads as one creature and sets you hunting for an ibex or a markhor. The adjective is not describing the goat at all; it is describing what to do with the letters of both words.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stone Age is the long prehistoric stretch named for the material its tools were made from, before metal was worked.

clue.text: Sweet nothing when alpha ousts husband

indicators.note: To oust somebody is to drive them out and stand in their place, so one letter leaves and the other takes the very same spot.

parts.note: nought is nothing spelled out as a word, the zero itself
H is the standard abbreviation for husband, and it is the letter driven out
alpha is the Greek A, and the same letter in the pilots' alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet nothing' is a whispered endearment, and that is exactly the reading to drop: 'sweet' is the definition on its own and 'nothing' is a word to be written out and then meddled with.
explanation.definitionFit: Nougat is the chewy confection of sugar, honey and nuts, so it belongs to the general class the definition names.

clue.text: Poor stooge and journalist decline through neglect

indicators.note: A poor effort is a botched one, and letters botched have been put down in the wrong arrangement.

parts.note: six letters for the shuffle; a stooge is a comedian's fall guy
ED is the crossword's editor, the journalist who runs the desk

explanation.walkthrough: A garden nobody tends runs to seed and stops flowering, which is where the phrase for decay comes from. 'Poor stooge' asks for sympathy; it is an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to seed is to run down through being left alone — a plant bolting when nobody tends it, said of people too.

clue.text: Mentioned rugby forward's pipe

indicators.note: Something merely mentioned is spoken rather than written, so what counts is the sound of the word and not its spelling.

parts.note: the man in the middle of the front row, who hooks the ball back with his foot; in most British speech that final R is not sounded

explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British English the two words are a single sound, which is the whole trick. 'Pipe' is the water pipe of a Middle Eastern café rather than anything plumbers fit.
explanation.definitionFit: A hookah is the water pipe smoked through a long flexible tube, so the definition names it by its general kind.

clue.text: Locksmith that's scored?

definitions.meaning: the surface offers the tradesman who cuts keys; the locks meant are the ones on a head, and this is the man who deals with those
not a goal but a musical score — the man in question is the hero of a Rossini opera, written out for voices and orchestra

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Locksmith' as a trade practised on hair and 'scored' as set to music, and you land on Rossini's comic opera about Figaro, the scheming barber of a Spanish city. The question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the opera: its hero cuts hair for a living, and the work itself exists as a score.

clue.text: On which being in a union is often indicated

definitions.meaning: the surface suggests a trade union and a membership card; the union the setter means is a marriage
the sign is worn rather than announced, and 'often' concedes that not everybody wears one

explanation.walkthrough: The union is a marriage rather than a trade union, and the answer is a place rather than a thing: in Britain the fourth finger of the left hand, where the band goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A band worn on that one finger is the customary sign of being married, so the clue names the digit by what wearing it announces.

clue.text: Component of engine dirt ruined

indicators.note: A ruined building has had its parts knocked out of place, and letters ruined are letters no longer in their original arrangement.

parts.note: six letters for the pile, taken from the machine's name and not its meaning
the remaining four, which supply the second I and the only R

explanation.walkthrough: 'Component of engine' reads as a car part and sends you hunting for pistons and valves. The words are only letters, and what they build belongs in a kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingredient is one of the parts a mixture is made from, so it is a component of a recipe rather than of a machine.

clue.text: Ally ousts Republican devil

indicators.note: To oust is to force somebody out of a position they held, so the letter named is driven out of the word and nothing comes in for it.

parts.note: an ally is a friend, the word taken at full length before anything is removed
R is the standard abbreviation for Republican, as printed on a US ballot paper

explanation.walkthrough: American politics supplies both the letter and the picture: read straight, the clue is one party's man pushing another out of office. Only the single R actually goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiend is a demon or evil spirit, which is precisely what 'devil' names — the same infernal creature under another word.

clue.text: Clergyman cut grass border

indicators.note: Something cut has had a piece taken off its end, so the word loses its final letter.

parts.note: the church officer who looks after the building and carries the mace ahead of the clergy in procession

explanation.walkthrough: A verger is strictly a lay official rather than an ordained man, so 'clergyman' is a shade loose and the setter is trading on the church setting. On British roads the strip of grass beside the tarmac is the verge.
explanation.definitionFit: A verge is the strip of grass running along the edge of a British road, so it is literally a border made of grass.

clue.text: Article more dodgy — it requires proof

definitions.note: The setter defines by description rather than by synonym: 'it' stands in for the answer, so the phrase says what the thing needs instead of naming it.

indicators.note: A dodgy character cannot be trusted to stay where he is put, and letters called dodgy will not keep their order either.

parts.note: the definite article itself, spelled out in full
the same four letters, resettled into another order

explanation.walkthrough: The dash works as an equals sign: everything to its left builds the word and everything to its right describes it. 'Article' is the grammarian's term, not a piece in a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A theorem is a mathematical statement that counts for nothing until it has been proved, so needing a proof is what makes it one.

clue.text: Votes against suppressing super chats

indicators.note: To suppress something is to hold it down out of sight, so the word doing the suppressing closes over the one that disappears.

parts.note: in a debate the cons are the votes against, the other half of the pros
fab is sixties British slang for marvellous, and 'super' is the same praise a generation earlier

explanation.walkthrough: 'Suppressing super chats' reads as a moderator deleting messages, which is the wrong picture entirely: 'chats' is the definition, and 'super' is only there as dated slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A confab is an informal chat or friendly discussion, short for confabulation, so the plural matches a plural definition.

clue.text: Overseas capital gains initially put into Barclays? All right

indicators.note: Initially means at the very start, so only the opening letter of the word beside it is wanted.
To put one thing into another is to place it bodily inside, so the single letter lands within the word that follows.

parts.note: Barclays is one of the British high-street banks, and the question mark admits it is only an example of the general word
just the initial letter of the word, which is all that is asked for
OK is the everyday spelling of 'all right' used as assent

explanation.walkthrough: 'Overseas capital gains' reads as a tax phrase, and that is the trap: the definition stops at 'capital', and 'gains' is in the clue for its first letter alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Bangkok is the capital of Thailand, and 'overseas' does the work of saying the city wanted is a foreign one rather than a British one.

clue.text: Capacity to talk big: 'get off that,' he exploded

indicators.note: An exploded object has been blown apart and its bits scattered, so the letters come to rest in a new arrangement.

parts.note: three letters for the pile — the word is not describing the talking
the quoted shout supplies ten more letters, punctuation ignored
the pronoun is fodder too, easy to miss because it reads as the person doing the shouting

explanation.walkthrough: 'Talk big' is the phrase the surface hands you, and 'big' belongs to the letters instead — which is why the count reaches fifteen only once you include it and the stray 'he'.
explanation.definitionFit: The gift of the gab is the knack of fluent, persuasive talking, so the definition names the ability rather than any one speech.

clue.text: Sick owners deteriorate

indicators.note: Somebody sick is out of sorts and not himself, so letters described that way are not in their proper state either.

parts.note: the six letters of the people in the surface, resettled into another word

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a landlord with a bad cold. 'Sick' is not describing him at all; it is describing what has to happen to the six letters that follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: To worsen is to grow worse or make worse, which is exactly what deteriorating is — the same verb in shorter clothes.

clue.text: For some, Jupiter rises in Middle Eastern port

indicators.note: A down entry read upwards runs from its foot to its head, and anything that rises travels in exactly that direction.

parts.note: the Romans' Jupiter is the Greeks' Zeus, and 'for some' marks that change of pantheon; those four letters are then read from the bottom up

explanation.walkthrough: Two names, one god: only the Greek one is any use here, and 'for some' is the setter's quiet signal to make the swap. The port sits at the southern mouth of the canal.
explanation.definitionFit: Suez is the Egyptian town at the Red Sea end of the canal that carries its name, which places it firmly in the Middle East.

clue.text: Passionate love for bird

parts.note: a flaming row is a passionate one — the adjective for anything blazing with feeling
in tennis love is a score of nothing, and nothing is written as a circle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Passionate love' looks like a single idea and the setter wants it as two, a fiery adjective followed by a tennis nought. 'For' is nothing but a joint.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is the bare category: a tall pink wading bird of salt lakes, offered as one bird among many.

clue.text: Sadly, dish of cold vegetables mostly thrown up

indicators.note: in a down clue, sent upwards, so the letters read from bottom to top
most but not all of the word, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: a salad is a dish of cold, usually raw, vegetables

explanation.surface: A sorry tale of a salad that was largely vomited back up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' cuts SALAD to SALA, and 'thrown up' reverses it in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Alas is an interjection expressing sorrow, used much as 'sadly' is used to introduce bad news.

clue.text: Cancel permit to enter river

indicators.note: To enter a building is to pass inside it, so the word for permission goes within the river's letters rather than beside them.

parts.note: the Dee, which runs through Chester and Aberdeen — a river crosswords keep on hand for its three letters
to let somebody do a thing is to permit it

explanation.walkthrough: Rivers are the crossword's small change and this is one of the commonest, so 'river' promises three letters before you know which three. The surface, a licence for a boat, is pure decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: To delete something is to cancel it out of a document or a list, the two verbs doing the same job to a piece of writing.

clue.text: Clever clogs needing support with primary email folder?

parts.note: the undergarment is the crossword's usual support, and the only one that comes in three letters
the folder new mail lands in first, which is what 'primary' is pointing at

explanation.walkthrough: 'Clever clogs' is British for a show-off know-all, said half in affection. The support is underwear rather than a bracket, and that swap is the whole joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A brainbox is an informal British word for somebody very clever, which is what a clever clogs is, teasing tone included.
